zone: Wild Sky Wilderness — the Beckler, Barclay Creek and Sultan Basin approaches
_areas_note: Three unrelated road systems, all leaving US 2 in the lower Skykomish valley but sharing nothing once you turn off the highway. The Beckler River road (FR 65) north from a mile east of Skykomish, then left onto the Index-Galena road (FR 63) along the North Fork Skykomish, serves Spire Mountain — the climb leaves the road itself at a snowplow turnaround about 4.6 miles in, with no trail at any point. The Barclay Creek road (FR 6024, north from Baring) serves Tailgunner: the climbers' path leaves the road roughly a tenth of a mile below the Barclay Lake trailhead, the same path that serves Gunn Peak and Wing Peak. The Sultan Basin road north from Sultan, then Olney Creek road, serves Mount Stickney and is a different drive of some thirty miles from the other two. Mount Stickney is KEPT here because it is a lower Skykomish peak with no other zone, but be clear that it is served by NONE of the Beckler, Index-Galena or Reiter roads. NOT DUPLICATED from the existing Skykomish US 2 zone: Barclay Lake itself, Eagle Lake, the Lake Serene basin, Money Creek Campground, Beckler River Campground and Troublesome Creek Campground are all written there and are deliberately absent here. EXCLUDED: Sheep Gap Mountain is REMOVED — it is climbed from Barlow Pass on the Mountain Loop Highway via Gothic Basin or Weden Lake, an approach on the far side of the range with no connection to any road in this file, and its camps (Gothic Basin and Foggy Lake, Monte Cristo townsite, Barlow Pass) are already written in the Mountain Loop zone. Philadelphia Mountain is REMOVED — it is a ridge scramble east from Lake Serene, reached from the Mount Index Road (FR 6020) and the Lake Serene trailhead, which is the anchor trailhead of the existing Skykomish US 2 zone; its only camping option is the Lake Serene basin, already written there, so it belongs in that file rather than this one.

sites.name: Gunn Basin, below Tailgunner Pass
sites.capacity: Open heather benches and slabs holding perhaps three or four small tents, scattered rather than clustered. No constructed sites, no toilet, no fire ring worth using.
sites.water: Snowmelt tarns in the basin through midsummer, and a small stream draining the pass. Both can dry to nothing by late August in a thin year — carry the day's water up from Barclay Creek if the season has been hot.
sites.permit: Wild Sky Wilderness, no permit or quota for camping. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at the Barclay Lake trailhead and at the pullouts either side of it. Stoves rather than fires — the basin is at the edge of timberline and the scattered wood there is what holds the heather together.
sites.notes: This is the high camp for Tailgunner, and it turns a very long day into a comfortable one. The climbers' path leaves the Barclay Creek road below the Barclay Lake trailhead, crosses the creek, and then climbs relentlessly and steeply through forest on a faint boot track, with dirt-covered slabs, a narrow traverse under cliffs and an exposed crossing above a waterfall before the angle relents into the basin. Reckon on three to four hours to camp with overnight loads. From here Tailgunner itself is an easy hour of slabby scrambling, and Gunn Peak and Wing Peak are both within reach the same morning, which is the usual reason parties carry a camp up at all. The shoulder of Tailgunner holds a shallow tarn perched right on the lip of the drop, and it is the obvious place to put a tent, but it is exposed and there is nothing between it and the weather. Season is roughly July to early October; earlier than that the traverse under the cliffs holds hard snow and the waterfall crossing is genuinely dangerous. The approach path is not maintained, is easy to lose on the descent, and should be tracked on the way up.

sites.name: Barclay Creek roadhead pullouts
sites.capacity: A handful of rough dispersed pullouts and one small clearing on a spur road a short walk below the trailhead. Room for two or three vehicles to sleep beside, not a campground.
sites.water: Barclay Creek runs beside the road and is the only supply. Treat it.
sites.permit: National forest, dispersed camping, no permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the trailhead parking itself. Campfire restrictions follow the district and are common from July onward — check before assuming a fire is legal.
sites.notes: This is a staging camp rather than a destination, and it exists in this file because the Tailgunner and Gunn climbers' path leaves the road here rather than at the lake. Sleeping at the roadhead lets a party start the steep forest climb in the dark and reach the basin before the day heats up, which matters on a south-facing approach. The spur road with the clearing drops off the main road a short distance below the pit toilet at the Barclay Lake trailhead; the path itself heads right before that clearing and is unsigned. Do not confuse this with Barclay Lake, which is a maintained walk-in with established lakeside sites and is covered elsewhere. The road is plowed nowhere and is gated by snow from roughly late November to April, which puts the winter ascent of Tailgunner well out of reach for most parties. Expect log trucks and weekend traffic through the summer, and expect the trailhead lot to be full by mid-morning on any fine Saturday.

sites.name: Spire Mountain — the saddle northwest of the summit
sites.capacity: One or two parties at most, on whatever flat ground the ridge crest offers. There is no established site here and nothing has been built.
sites.water: None. There is no water anywhere on this route once you leave the North Fork Skykomish at the road, and the saddle holds nothing but lingering snow patches into July. Carry everything, or melt snow early season.
sites.permit: Wild Sky Wilderness, no permit required. Parking is a roadside pullout, so no forest pass is needed there.
sites.notes: Spire Mountain has no established camping of any kind and most parties climb it in a single very long day, which is the honest answer. The route is entirely off-trail: leave the Index-Galena road at the snowplow turnaround just past the bridge, drop south into old forest, and fight through six hundred feet of steep ground choked with fallen timber before the slope becomes merely steep. Cliffs on the north end of the mountain are turned between about 4,200 and 4,400 feet, then a rising traverse southeast reaches open ground around 5,400 feet below the summit spire. The saddle above that, northwest of the true summit, is the only ground on the route flat enough to lie down on, and a party that has misjudged the day will end up there whether they planned to or not. From it the last three hundred feet are technical enough that most rope up for short exposed sections. ROAD STATUS IS THE LIMITING FACTOR: the Index-Galena road has repeatedly been cut by flood damage and bridge failure on the North Fork Skykomish, and when the bridge is out the road is simply not drivable from the Beckler River road, which adds many miles of walking to an approach that is already brutal. Confirm the road is open before committing to this peak. Best season is late July to early October, once the timber is dry and before the first storms make the traverse slabs greasy.

sites.name: San Juan Campground, Index-Galena road
sites.capacity: A small forest campground of a dozen or so sites in second-growth beside the North Fork Skykomish, with vault toilets and no water system.
sites.water: River water only, treated. There is no potable supply.
sites.permit: Standard national forest campground fee when it is operating. No wilderness permit is involved at this elevation.
sites.notes: The nearest developed camp to the Spire Mountain roadhead, sitting on the Index-Galena road a few miles below where the climb starts. It spent close to two decades unreachable by vehicle after flood damage took out the road, and access has been restored and lost again more than once since; treat its availability as a question to answer before you drive rather than an assumption. When the road is cut at the North Fork bridge it is unreachable from the Beckler River side entirely. Even when it is open it is a low, damp, mosquito-heavy site in early summer, and its value is convenience rather than pleasure — it puts a party within twenty minutes of the start of the Spire approach, which is worth a great deal on a climb that wants a pre-dawn departure. Beckler River Campground and Troublesome Creek Campground serve the same road system and are covered in the neighbouring zone, so check those first if this one is closed.

sites.name: One Acre Lake, under Mount Stickney
sites.capacity: A few flat spots on the benches around a small tarn, informal and unimproved. Two or three tents.
sites.water: The lake, and snowmelt in the drainages above it well into July. Treat everything; the basin is shallow and the water warms.
sites.permit: No wilderness permit — this is outside the Wild Sky boundary on a mix of state and federal land. No pass at the gated roadhead. Fires are a poor idea in a basin this small and are restricted through most summers.
sites.notes: The one place worth camping on Mount Stickney, and the reason the peak is doable at all now that the road is gated low. The route leaves the Sultan Basin road onto the old Olney Creek logging road, which used to let a high-clearance vehicle grind up to around 2,100 feet and is now closed at its very beginning, so the road walk is five to six miles before any climbing starts. Where the road levels near 3,700 feet a trail cuts off to the right along a ridge; leave that around 4,050 feet and traverse southeast to the lake. From camp the route continues southeast past a set of tarns near 4,500 feet, up to about 4,800, and then traverses into the boulder basin below the summit, taking a gully just west of the top to gain the crest. THIS IS A WINTER AND EARLY SPRING PEAK by preference, not a summer one: the low western start means it comes into condition when everything else is buried, and deep snow covers a boulder field that is loose, awkward and slow when bare. The trade is that the same snow brings real avalanche exposure on the traverses above the lake, and early-season parties have found route-finding and slope assessment to be the hard part rather than the climbing. Expect a long day either way, and expect the road walk to feel longer on the way out.

sites.name: Sultan Basin road pullouts and the Olney Creek gate
sites.capacity: Gravel pullouts and a turnaround at the gate. Room to sleep in or beside a vehicle, nothing more. No toilet, no table, no fire ring you should trust.
sites.water: Olney Creek, a short way along the closed road, where a spur drops to a bridge and a gravel bar. Treat it.
sites.permit: Mixed state and municipal watershed land, with day-use restrictions posted in places and gates that change. Read the signs at the gate rather than assuming dispersed camping is permitted where you have parked. Fire restrictions here are usually stricter than on national forest and are enforced.
sites.notes: A pure staging pullout for Mount Stickney, included because the road walk is now long enough that starting it at first light matters. From US 2 in Sultan, the Sultan Basin road runs north for roughly eleven and a half miles before the Olney Creek road turns off on the right, and the gate is at the very start of that turn. Sleeping at the gate saves an hour of driving in the dark and puts the five-to-six mile approach march in the coolest part of the morning. The Sultan Basin road is paved for its lower miles and gravel above; it is generally drivable in a normal car to the gate, but conditions after a wet winter are worth checking. This is working forest and watershed land rather than recreation land, so expect industrial traffic, expect gates to move, and do not count on a pullout being available where it was last year. There is no established camping anywhere between here and One Acre Lake.
